definition:
The doctrine of humanity (theologians call it theological anthropology, from the Greek anthrōpos, ‘human being’) is what Scripture teaches about what we are. Its first answer is that human beings are creatures: made by God, dependent on him for every breath, formed from the same dust as the rest of the living world. Its second is that among the creatures they are set apart, made in the image of God, male and female, to know him, to love one another, and to rule and tend the earth under him as his representatives. Its third is that this creature has fallen and is now damaged by sin, yet never stops bearing God's image, so that every human life carries a dignity no one can grant or revoke. Its last is that Jesus Christ is the true human being, the image of God in person, and that God's purpose is to remake a people in his likeness, body and soul, in the resurrection. The meaning of the image itself, the fall and the nature of sin, marriage and sexuality, and work each have their own studies; this one follows the whole biblical portrait of the human creature, and the site's page on body and soul sets out the views on how a person is constituted.

The vocabulary is concrete. The Hebrew ’adam means ‘humankind’ or ‘a human being’ and becomes the first man's name; it sounds like ’adamah, ‘ground’, a wordplay Genesis 2:7 uses to say that the human is an earth creature, not an explanation of where the word came from. Tselem, ‘image’, is elsewhere a statue or likeness of something, and demut, ‘likeness’, means resemblance; Genesis 1:26 uses both, and most Hebrew scholars read them as overlapping rather than as two different gifts. Nephesh, often translated ‘soul’, most often means a living being, a life, or the self, and can even mean ‘throat’ or ‘appetite’; animals are also a living nephesh (Genesis 1:30 uses it of them). Ruach is breath, wind, or spirit; basar is flesh, human life in its frailty; lev, the ‘heart’, is the center of thought, will, and desire more than of emotion. The New Testament Greek terms carry similar ranges: psychē (life, self, soul), pneuma (spirit), sōma (body, the whole person as embodied), sarx (flesh, sometimes in Paul humanity turned against God), kardia (heart), and eikōn (image). None of these words, in either language, names a detachable part in every use; they are ways of looking at one whole person from different sides.
ot:
Scripture's portrait of humanity begins with two accounts of creation that look at the same creature from two angles. In Genesis 1 humanity is the last and climactic work of the six days, and God deliberates before making it: “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness, to rule over the fish of the sea” (Genesis 1:26). The next verse says it three times, in poetic parallel: “So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). Humanity is made as two sexes together, blessed, told to be fruitful and fill the earth, and given dominion over the creatures; the rule is that of a steward, since the same chapter gives them only plants for food (Genesis 1:29). In the ancient Near East, kings set up statues of themselves in conquered lands, and Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts call a king the image of a god. Genesis gives that royal title to every man and woman. Only after humanity is made does God call all he has made “very good” (Genesis 1:31).

Genesis 2 moves in close. “The LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being” (Genesis 2:7). The verse does not say the man received a soul but that he became a nephesh, a living being, by God's breath animating dust. He is placed in the garden “to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15), so work belongs to creation before any curse, and he is given a command with a limit, which makes him a moral creature who can obey or refuse. Then, for the first time, something is “not good”: the man is alone (Genesis 2:18). The woman is made as “a suitable helper”, a phrase using ‘ezer, a word the Old Testament most often uses of God himself as Israel's help (Psalm 121:1-2), so it implies no inferiority. The man's response is the first human poem, and the narrator draws out marriage: “they will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Humanity is made for God, for one another, and for the earth.

After the fall, the Old Testament never withdraws the image. Genesis 5 repeats that God made humanity in his likeness and then says Adam “had a son in his own likeness, after his own image” (Genesis 5:3), so the image passes on through the generations of a fallen race. After the flood, murder is forbidden “for in His own image God has made mankind” (Genesis 9:6); the image grounds the worth of every human life. The Law guards that worth in concrete ways: the stranger, the widow, the orphan, and even the slave have rights Israel must honor, and Proverbs says that “Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker” (Proverbs 14:31). Psalm 8 marvels at the same paradox Genesis sets up, the smallness of humanity under the stars and its crown of glory: “what is man that You are mindful of him” and yet “You crowned him with glory and honor” (Psalm 8:4-5). Psalm 139 extends God's care to life in the womb: “You knit me together in my mother’s womb” (Psalm 139:13).

The Old Testament is just as honest about human frailty. Human beings are dust and breath, and when God withdraws breath they return to dust (Psalm 104:29). God “is mindful that we are dust” and our days are like grass (Psalm 103:14-15); Isaiah hears that “All flesh is like grass” while the word of God stands forever (Isaiah 40:6-8). Ecclesiastes adds that God made humanity upright, but “they have sought out many schemes” (Ecclesiastes 7:29), and that God “has also set eternity in the hearts of men” (Ecclesiastes 3:11), a longing no earthly thing satisfies. The prophets locate the human problem in the heart and promise a new one: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). The Old Testament thus leaves a creature of great dignity and great weakness, made to reflect God and failing to do so, waiting for God to restore what the fall defaced.
nt:
The New Testament's decisive word about humanity is Jesus. He shares our humanity completely (“He too shared in their humanity”, Hebrews 2:14), grows in wisdom and stature (Luke 2:52), hungers, weeps, and dies. Pilate's words at his trial, “Here is the man” (John 19:5), carry for John's readers a meaning Pilate did not intend. Jesus treats human worth as greater than religious rules (“The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath”, Mark 2:27) and tells his disciples they are “worth more than many sparrows” (Matthew 10:31). When asked about marriage, he goes back to creation: “from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female’” (Mark 10:6), joining Genesis 1:27 and 2:24. The whole human person, heart, soul, mind, and strength, is summoned to love God, and the neighbor is to be loved as oneself (Mark 12:30-31). When shown a coin, he asks, “Whose image is this?” (Matthew 22:20); many interpreters have heard in his answer the implication that what bears God's image belongs to God.

Paul places all of humanity under two heads. Adam, “The first man”, was “of the dust of the earth”; Christ is “the last Adam” and “the second man from heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:45-47). In Athens Paul tells the philosophers that “From one man He made every nation of men” and that “He is not far from each one of us” (Acts 17:26-27), grounding the unity of the human race and every people's dignity in creation. The New Testament then calls Christ himself the image of God: “Christ, who is the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4) and “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), using eikōn, the Septuagint's word for the image in Genesis 1. What Adam was made to be, Christ is. Salvation is therefore a restoration of the image: God predestined his people “to be conformed to the image of His Son” (Romans 8:29), and believers “are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Colossians describes the new self “being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator”, a renewal in which the divisions of race and class fall away (Colossians 3:10-11), and Ephesians says it is “created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness” (Ephesians 4:24).

The New Testament also refuses to treat the body as a husk. Believers are to offer their bodies as living sacrifices (Romans 12:1), and Paul tells the Corinthians, who thought what they did with their bodies did not matter, that “your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit” and that they must “glorify God with your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Paul can speak of the person as spirit, soul, and body (1 Thessalonians 5:23), and Hebrews of the word “dividing soul and spirit” (Hebrews 4:12), though whether these texts describe separable parts or the whole person from several sides is debated. James forbids cursing people “who have been made in God’s likeness” (James 3:9), showing that the image remains in fallen humanity. Hebrews reads Psalm 8 of Jesus: we do not yet see all things subject to humanity, “But we see Jesus”, crowned with glory because he suffered death (Hebrews 2:8-9).

The goal is bodily. Believers wait for “the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23), when Christ “will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). Paul contrasts the body sown perishable with the body “raised imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:42), and John says that “we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2). The last picture of humanity in the Bible is of people who see God's face, bear his name, and “reign forever and ever” (Revelation 22:4-5). The dominion given in Genesis 1 and lost in Genesis 3 is given back to a redeemed humanity in Christ.

keyTexts.why: God makes humanity in his image and likeness, male and female, blessed and given dominion over the earth. The foundation of every Christian teaching about human dignity.
The LORD forms the man from dust and breathes into him, and he becomes a living being. Humanity is earthly and God-breathed at once, a unity rather than a soul lodged in a body.
The man is placed in the garden to work and keep it, given a command, and joined to the woman. Work, moral responsibility, and relationship belong to humanity before the fall.
After the flood, killing a human being is forbidden because humanity is made in God's image. The image survives the fall and grounds the sanctity of life.
Humanity is small under the heavens yet crowned with glory and set over God's works. Hebrews 2 reads it of Jesus, the true human.
God remembers that we are dust; our days are like grass. The frailty of humanity met by the compassion of a father.
God forms the psalmist in the womb and knows him before birth. Human life is known and valued by God from its beginning.
God made humanity upright, but people have sought out many schemes. A one-line summary of creation and fall.
Jesus distinguishes killing the body from destroying the soul and says his disciples are worth more than many sparrows. A key text for both human worth and the body-soul question.
Paul tells Athens that God made every nation from one man and that in him we live and move. The unity and dependence of the whole human race.
The first Adam was from the dust; the last Adam is from heaven, and we will bear his likeness in a raised, imperishable body.
Believers are being transformed into the image of the Lord from glory to glory by the Spirit. Salvation as the restoring of the image.
Christ is the image of the invisible God. What humanity was made to be, he is.
The new self is renewed in the image of its Creator, in a community where ethnic and social divisions no longer rule.
It is wrong to curse people because they are made in God's likeness. The image remains in fallen humanity and governs how we speak of anyone.

history:
The early church defended the goodness of the body and the unity of the person against Gnostic teachers who treated matter as a prison. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies, about 180) insisted that the whole human being, flesh included, is God's handiwork and will be saved, and in book 5 he distinguished the image, which all humans have, from the likeness, a spiritual endowment restored by the Spirit; many later Eastern theologians kept a form of that distinction. Tertullian's On the Soul (early third century) argued that the soul is passed on from parents with the body (traducianism), while Jerome held that God creates each soul directly (creationism); Augustine never decided between them. Gregory of Nyssa's On the Making of Man (379) developed the image as the royal dignity and freedom of the human mind, and in his fourth homily on Ecclesiastes he condemned slaveholding as a claim to own what bears God's image, a rare ancient voice against the institution. Augustine's On the Trinity (completed about 420) located the image in the mind, reflecting the Trinity in its memory, understanding, and will, and his Confessions (about 400) described the restless heart made for God.

Medieval theology built on Augustine. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I, question 93) placed the image in humanity's intellectual nature and distinguished three degrees of it, by nature, by grace, and by glory. The Council of Vienne (1312) defined that the rational soul is of itself the form of the human body, and the Fifth Lateran Council (1513) condemned the teaching that the individual soul is mortal. The Reformers read the image more relationally and more tragically. Luther, in his Lectures on Genesis (1535 to 1545), rejected the distinction between image and likeness and identified the image with the original righteousness lost at the fall, while Calvin (Institutes, book 1, chapter 15) held that the image shines chiefly in the soul but extends to the whole person, and after the fall is not wholly destroyed but horribly deformed. When European conquest of the Americas raised the question whether Indigenous peoples were fully human, Pope Paul III's bull Sublimis Deus (1537) declared them rational persons who must not be enslaved, and the Dominican Bartolomé de las Casas argued the same against Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda at the Valladolid debate (1550 to 1551). The church's record was far worse than those statements, but the argument against the slave trade that followed drew heavily on the image of God.

Modern theology has pursued three readings of the image. Karl Barth (Church Dogmatics III/1, 1945) read it as relationship, humanity as male and female reflecting the relational life of God. Old Testament scholars such as Gerhard von Rad and D. J. A. Clines (in a 1968 article, ‘The Image of God in Man’) emphasized the royal and representative sense drawn from the ancient Near East, a view J. Richard Middleton developed in The Liberating Image (2005). Roman Catholic teaching at the Second Vatican Council, in Gaudium et Spes (1965), taught that the meaning of humanity is made clear only in Christ, the incarnate Word. Debates over human origins after Darwin led Pope Pius XII, in Humani Generis (1950), to allow inquiry into the origin of the human body while holding that souls are created directly by God. Contemporary Christian bioethics, from the beginning of life to its end, and Christian advocacy for the disabled and the unborn, rest on the conviction that the image is not a capacity some humans have more of than others but the status of every human being before God.

differ.view: What is the image of God?
differ.body: The structural view, from Irenaeus, Augustine, and Aquinas, holds that the image consists in capacities that set humanity apart, especially reason, conscience, and freedom. The relational view, associated with Karl Barth and Emil Brunner, holds that it consists in being made for relationship with God and one another, shown in the pairing of male and female in Genesis 1:27. The functional or royal view, argued by D. J. A. Clines and J. Richard Middleton, holds that it names humanity's calling to represent God's rule on earth, since Genesis 1:26 ties the image directly to dominion. Many theologians now hold these as aspects of one reality. The study of the image of God treats this question in detail.

differ.view: How is a human person constituted?
differ.body: Most of the church's tradition has held a form of dualism: a human being is body and soul, deeply united in this life but separable at death, which explains the conscious presence with Christ that Luke 23:43 and Philippians 1:23 promise; John W. Cooper's Body, Soul, and Life Everlasting (1989) defends a dualism that stresses the unity of body and soul in this life. Thomists hold that the soul is the form of the body, one substance that persists incomplete after death. Trichotomists, such as Franz Delitzsch in the nineteenth century, distinguish spirit from soul (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Christian physicalists, such as Nancey Murphy in Bodies and Souls, or Spirited Bodies? (2006), hold that a person is a unified physical being and that the Christian hope rests on the resurrection, not on a naturally immortal soul. The site's page on body and soul sets these out in full.

differ.view: Where does each soul come from?
differ.body: Creationism of the soul (not to be confused with the debate over the age of the earth) holds that God creates each soul directly, most often said to be at conception; it has been the majority view in Roman Catholic and Reformed theology, and its defenders appeal to texts such as Ecclesiastes 12:7 and Hebrews 12:9. Traducianism holds that the whole person, soul and body, comes from the parents; Tertullian held it, many Lutheran theologians favored it, and its defenders argue that it explains the passing on of original sin and fits Genesis 5:3. Augustine weighed both and left the question open, and it remains open.

The church has traditionally read Adam and Eve as a historical first pair from whom all humans descend, and many theologians, such as C. John Collins in Did Adam and Eve Really Exist? (2011), argue that Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 requires a real Adam. Others hold that God brought humanity into being through a long process and chose or set apart an original pair or group within it, a range of views represented in William Lane Craig's In Quest of the Historical Adam (2021) and Denis Alexander's Creation or Evolution (2008). Still others read Adam chiefly as a representative figure for humanity. All affirm that humanity is made by God, bears his image, and has fallen.

errors:
The church has rejected any view that despises the body. The Gnostic teachers of the second century, and later the Manichaeans whom Augustine left, held that matter was evil and the spirit alone worth saving; the church answered with the goodness of creation, the incarnation, and the resurrection of the body. The opposite error, reducing a person to matter with no relation to God, is not a Christian option either, since Scripture holds that human beings live by God's breath and answer to him. The church has also rejected every attempt to rank human beings by race, sex, ability, or usefulness as if some bore God's image more fully than others. Genesis gives the image to ‘male and female’ alike, Acts 17:26 derives every nation from one, and the church's own failures here, in the slave trade and in racial segregation, are betrayals of what it confesses.

Two softer distortions are just as common. One inflates humanity, treating human beings as self-made and answerable to no one, which Scripture calls the root of the fall. The other deflates humanity, treating people as worthless because they are sinners, as though sin had erased the image. Scripture holds both truths together: humanity is fallen and still bears God's image (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9), and the depth of the fall is measured precisely by the height of what was lost.
life:
If every person bears God's image, then there are no ordinary people. The coworker who irritates, the stranger at the border, the child in the womb, the elderly parent who no longer remembers a name, and the enemy all carry a dignity that does not depend on what they can do or what they have done. That changes how a Christian speaks (James 3:9), how a Christian votes and spends and hires, and how a Christian cares for the weak. It also changes how a person regards themselves. Human beings are dust, and it is no shame to be tired, to grow old, or to need help; God “is mindful that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). Yet human beings are also crowned with glory, which means that no failure or illness or disability reduces a person to a thing.

The doctrine shapes hope most of all. The body is not a shell to be discarded but a gift to be offered to God now and raised by him at the last. Work, marriage, friendship, and rest are ways of living out the image, not distractions from spiritual life. And the pattern of a human life is not a climb toward becoming more than human but a slow remaking into the likeness of Jesus, the one person who has lived a truly human life, until at his appearing his people see him as he is.
questions: Genesis 1 describes humanity as royal image-bearers and Genesis 2 as dust animated by God's breath. How do these two pictures correct each other, and which one do you find it harder to believe about yourself?

James 3:9 says it is wrong to curse people because they are made in God's likeness. What would change in your speech, habits, or public life if you took that verse seriously about the people you find hardest to respect?

The New Testament calls Christ the true image of God and says believers are being transformed into his image. What does it look like to become more fully human rather than less, and where have you seen that in someone's life?
